One-sentence judgment: a Commercial Diver is not just going down to take a look, but inspecting, repairing, removing, or installing equipment and structures below the surface using surface-supplied or scuba equipment, possibly using power and hand tools such as drills, sledgehammers, cutting torches, and welding equipment, and possibly conducting tests or experiments, placing explosives, or photographing structures or marine life; O*NET defines this occupation as working below the surface of the water using surface-supplied or scuba equipment to inspect, repair, remove, or install equipment and structures; possibly using a variety of power and hand tools (such as drills, sledgehammers, and cutting torches and welding equipment); and possibly conducting tests or experiments, placing explosives, or photographing structures or marine life; this page follows the O*NET-SOC 49-9092.00 precise occupational basis.

Signal to keep exploring: you are willing to complete every step under the constraints of equipment, gas, duration, and depth, and to accept that the working environment (weather, current, visibility, noise) is itself uncontrollable; O*NET work context shows 87% work outdoors under all weather conditions, 87% have continuous contact with others, 83% wear common protective or safety equipment every day, 77% have face-to-face discussions every day, 73% consider working with a work group or team extremely important, 69% have very high responsibility for the health and safety of others (with a further 17% at high responsibility), 62% work in an enclosed vehicle or equipment, 61% continuously use hands to handle tools or controls, 53% wear specialized protective equipment (such as a respirator) every day, and 52% face time pressure more than once a week.

The work of a Commercial Diver can be divided into three connected but independent work surfaces. The first is underwater inspection and testing: inspecting and testing docks, ships, buoy systems, intakes or outfalls, or underwater pipelines, cables, and sewers (closed-circuit television may be used); inspecting the condition of underwater steel or wood structures; operating underwater video, sonar, recording, or related equipment to investigate underwater structures or marine life; sampling or photographing to assess the condition of ships or structures; and performing non-destructive testing (for example, testing offshore drilling platform legs for cracks). The second is underwater repair and installation work: using underwater welding equipment, clamps, and supports to cut and weld steel; using caulking materials, bolts, and hand tools to repair underwater hulls, bridge foundations, or other structures; installing, inspecting, cleaning, or repairing pipelines or valves; setting or directing the placement of piles or sandbags to support structures such as docks, bridges, cofferdams, or platforms; installing piles or footings for docks or bridges; and using pneumatic or power hand tools to clear obstructions from screens or from shipways and launching ways. The third is salvage, search and rescue, and special operations: taking part in underwater search and rescue, salvage, recovery, or cleanup operations; lifting sunken objects by rigging, attaching the rigging to the crane line, and operating winches, booms, or cranes; using pneumatic and hydraulic tools to salvage sunken vessels or their cargo, using explosives when necessary; drilling into rock and placing explosives for underwater blasting; removing surface debris or pollution; taking on offshore oil and gas exploration or production tasks (such as conducting underwater surveys or repairing and maintaining drilling platform equipment); and raising or harvesting marine species at fish farms or completing daily operations there.

Using surface-supplied or scuba equipment to inspect, repair, remove, or install equipment and structures below the surface, and using power and hand tools and underwater welding and testing equipment to complete the work

Editorial summarized flow: confirm the task environment → verify equipment, personnel, and plan → complete registration and pre-planning per the applicable requirements → enter the water and communicate and work with the tender and team → record per plan, decompress, exit and check, and hand over; decompression may occur during or after the dive and is not uniformly written as only after exiting the water.

Turn underwater work into deliverable results in which equipment, gas, and duration are controlled, communication and escalation are unobstructed, and inspection conclusions and repair records are reviewable

Editorial process summary: task and environment verification, equipment and plan checks, team-assisted work and communication, depth and time and result records, decompression per the applicable plan, and post-dive checks and handover; no operating steps are provided.

US 1910.422(e) requires a depth and time record for each diver including applicable gas changes and decompression; 423(d) requires that each operation record the personnel, date, time, and place, the mode, the tasks, the approximate environment, the maximum depth, and the bottom time, with additional profile, decompression, and treatment records applicable as conditions require. The 440 retention period differs by record type and event; inspection, repair, and handover records are task-related editorial recommendations, and not all fields are written as uniformly mandatory in every jurisdiction.

Six recurring occupational judgments: whether equipment, gas supply, duration, and decompression are verified per plan; whether surface communication and signals are available throughout; whether underwater working conditions (weather, current, visibility, structural condition) meet the start conditions; whether welding, cutting, non-destructive testing, and blasting are within the authorized and specified scope; whether lifting, rigging, and salvage are carried out per the load and signal agreements; and whether inspection and repair records and handover are reviewable.
Judgment one: whether equipment, gas supply, duration, and decompression are verified per plan

Before real work, the authorized role verifies the equipment, gas supply, and plan per the applicable manual; anomaly handling follows approved procedures, and this page provides no underwater emergency, ascent and descent, or decompression parameters.
Judgment two: whether surface communication and signals are available throughout

The surface communication method, tending, and interruption handling must be confirmed per the applicable diving mode and approved procedures; underwater actions cannot be decided on one's own from an occupational overview.
Judgment three: whether underwater working conditions meet the start conditions

Treat weather, current, visibility, water temperature, and structural condition as preconditions for starting work; when conditions exceed the plan scope, decide together with the surface supervisor to postpone or switch to an alternative and record the decision and its basis.
Judgment four: whether welding, cutting, testing, and blasting are within the authorized and specified scope

Underwater welding, cutting, non-destructive testing, and blasting must be carried out with the corresponding qualifications and authorization and confirmed per operating standards and employer procedures for parameters and environmental requirements; work beyond one's authorization is escalated for confirmation first and not undertaken on the basis of experience alone.
Judgment five: whether lifting, rigging, and salvage are carried out per the load and signal agreements

Before lifting and rigging work, confirm the load, lifting points, rigging condition, and personnel exclusion zone, and follow the agreed signals and command flow; for overload, obstructed line of sight, or unclear signals, stop first and reconfirm.
Judgment six: whether inspection and repair records and handover are reviewable

Write out the work time, place, duration, depth, and gas, the inspection findings and testing methods, the repair and replacement content, and the anomalies and handling and escalation, so that the conclusions can be reviewed and traced by others rather than leaving only a verbal account.

A Commercial Diver uses surface-supplied or scuba equipment to inspect, repair, remove, or install equipment and structures below the surface. The work includes equipment maintenance, surface communication, inspection of underwater structures and pipelines, sampling, photography, and testing, repair and installation, and salvage; welding, cutting, lifting, blasting, and offshore oil and gas support are special operations carried out per task and authorization and are not undertaken in every position. Work plans, personnel qualifications, registration, and safety procedures must be verified per the applicable jurisdiction, mode, and employer requirements. The typical deliverables are inspection records, repair and installation records, and handover; structural safety or special operation conclusions must be confirmed by the correspondingly authorized role.

This page follows the precise occupational basis of O*NET-SOC 49-9092.00 (Commercial Divers; page updated 2026): this occupation works below the surface, using surface-supplied or scuba equipment to inspect, repair, remove, or install equipment and structures; it may use a variety of power and hand tools such as drills, sledgehammers, cutting torches, and welding equipment; and it may conduct tests or experiments, place explosives, or photograph structures or marine life. The current top three occupational interests are Realistic 100, Investigative 43, and Conventional 35, editorially abbreviated RIC (Realistic, Investigative, Conventional), and the preparation level is Job Zone Three (medium preparation); the page asks how much education a new entrant needs, and the respondent answers show 68% of respondents answered that a new entrant needs a postsecondary certificate, 23% answered that a new entrant needs an associate or other two-year degree, and 6% answered that a new entrant needs some college but no degree (the page shows only these three tiers); the occupation page marks this code with Bright Outlook.

paragraphs: The six directions share part of their abilities with this occupation: structural and mechanical common knowledge, tool and equipment operation, safety awareness, and on-site communication and record habits. The real difference lies in the environment and the responsibility: the design and calculation directions complete design and specification work on land, the manufacturing and installation directions complete assembly and welding in a controlled environment, the construction and laying directions complete physical and mechanical work on land, and the welding direction focuses on process quality; this occupation simultaneously carries underwater environment work, gas supply and duration and decompression constraints, and responsibility for its own and its companion's work safety. When choosing, it is suggested to first verify with a deliverable task sheet, equipment check, work, and record exercise, rather than comparing names first.

The comparison basis is the public tasks, work objects, and outputs of this occupation and the adjacent occupations; the links are for location, and the comparison is an editorial summary and does not constitute mutual recognition of qualifications, an operating permit, or a structural safety conclusion.

The table below compares the positions and occupations adjacent to this occupation: Ship Engineers and Marine Architects, Boilermakers, Construction Laborers, Operating Engineers and Other Construction Equipment Operators, Pipelayers, and Welders, Cutters, Solderers, and Brazers. The four columns answer the same kind of question: what this direction does, where the key difference from this occupation lies, and what kind of person is better suited to choose it.

Ship Engineers and Marine Architects focus on the design, calculation, and specification compliance of ships and marine structures, usually working on land or in a design department; this occupation performs inspection, repair, and installation underwater and is responsible for on-site gas supply and duration and safety.
People willing to do hull and marine structure design and calculation are suited to that direction; people willing to complete inspection and repair by hand underwater are suited to this occupation.
Mainly design proposals, calculations, and specification compliance documents.
Ship Engineers and Marine Architects

Boilermakers mainly assemble and weld large vessels, piping, and pressure parts on land or in a shipyard and work in a controlled environment; this occupation works in open water or water environments and must simultaneously handle gas supply and visibility and current limits.
People willing to assemble and weld large components in a workshop are suited to that direction; people willing to bring the same craft into the underwater environment are suited to this occupation.
Mainly component assembly and welding and inspection records.
Boilermakers

Construction Laborers focus on physical work, material handling, and assisting construction at land construction sites and do not carry underwater environment and gas supply and decompression responsibility; this occupation's working environment and safety constraints differ significantly.

People willing to do physical and assisting work at land construction sites are suited to that direction; people willing to accept underwater work constraints and obtain the corresponding qualifications are suited to this occupation.
Mainly construction sequence and site coordination records.
Construction Laborers

Operating Engineers and Other Construction Equipment Operators mainly operate excavation, lifting, and earthmoving construction machinery, usually above water or on land; this occupation mainly works by hand underwater and supports lifting and rigging work when needed.
People willing to operate large construction machinery are suited to that direction; people willing to center on underwater manual inspection and repair are suited to this occupation.
Mainly machinery operation and construction progress records.
Operating Engineers and Other Construction Equipment Operators
Pipelayers mainly excavate trenches and lay and connect pipelines on land; this occupation's pipeline and valve work is done underwater and must handle visibility, current, and gas supply limits.
People willing to do land pipeline laying and connection are suited to that direction; people willing to install and repair pipelines and valves underwater are suited to this occupation.
Mainly trench, laying, and pressure test records.
Pipelayers

Welders, Cutters, Solderers, and Brazers focus on welding process and quality control, usually working on land or in a workshop; this occupation must carry out similar work subject to meeting underwater welding specifications and authorization.

People willing to focus on welding process and quality are suited to that direction; people willing to take on underwater work after obtaining underwater welding qualifications are suited to this occupation.
Mainly welding process and inspection records.
Welders, Cutters, Solderers, and Brazers

Moving from this occupation to an adjacent direction usually requires adding new abilities and qualifications: the ship and marine architecture direction requires hull structure and design calculation and specification training; the boilermaking direction requires large component assembly and welding and inspection experience; the construction and site directions require land construction sequence and machinery coordination experience; the pipeline laying direction requires trench, connection, and pressure test experience; the welding direction requires welding process and inspection qualifications. Equipment operation and safety awareness are transferable, but the qualifications and working environment responsibility of each direction must be re-established.

entries.answer: A Commercial Diver uses surface-supplied or scuba equipment to inspect, repair, remove, or install equipment and structures below the surface. The work includes equipment maintenance, surface communication, inspection of underwater structures and pipelines, sampling, photography, and testing, repair and installation, and salvage; welding, cutting, lifting, blasting, and offshore oil and gas support are special operations carried out per task and authorization and are not undertaken in every position. Work plans, personnel qualifications, registration, and safety procedures must be verified per the applicable jurisdiction, mode, and employer requirements. The work context is an occupational survey and does not represent any one employer's daily arrangements.

entries.answer: Ship Engineers and Marine Architects focus on ship and marine structure design and calculation and do not work underwater; Boilermakers assemble and weld large vessels and piping in a controlled environment; Construction Laborers mainly do physical and assisting work at land construction sites; Operating Engineers and Other Construction Equipment Operators mainly operate construction machinery; Pipelayers mainly do land trenching and laying and connection; Welders, Cutters, Solderers, and Brazers focus on welding process and usually do not work underwater; this occupation simultaneously carries underwater environment work and gas supply and duration and decompression constraints and is responsible for work safety. Shared abilities do not mean interchangeability: the working environment, responsibility boundaries, and qualification requirements differ.

subject.name: Commercial Diver
subject.summary: A Commercial Diver uses surface-supplied or scuba equipment to inspect, repair, remove, or install equipment and structures below the surface. The work includes equipment maintenance, surface communication, inspection of underwater structures and pipelines, sampling, photography, and testing, repair and installation, and salvage; welding, cutting, lifting, blasting, and offshore oil and gas support are special operations carried out per task and authorization and are not undertaken in every position. Work plans, personnel qualifications, registration, and safety procedures must be verified per the applicable jurisdiction, mode, and employer requirements.
